title: Administration and Management of an ECCE Centre
summary: Administration is the process of running an organisation: making rules, taking decisions for stakeholders, managing operations, choosing staff, directing units towards goals and linking senior management with employees. Management is organising and coordinating all activities — policies, planning, organising, staffing, leading, controlling and allocating resources — to achieve the objectives. Management focuses on managing people and their work; administration on the best use of the organisation's resources. Both share the basic functions of planning, organising and controlling.

The administrator is responsible for the overall operation of the centre and its services; responsibilities are diverse and may be shared. Three levels of management: top (owners), middle (centre head and assistants) and first level (ECCE staff and teachers). Management styles: autocratic (most controlling), democratic, laissez-faire (least controlling). Management is responsible for directing and supervising staff; recruitment, induction, training and performance; the overall safety and well-being of children (physical and emotional); setting and implementing policies; complying with regulations; and managing and reporting finances. The Principal/Centre Head gives day-to-day management, helped by teachers, assistants, aides and support staff; the board of management includes owners' nominees, the head, teacher and parent representatives and community members.

The National ECCE Policy, 2013 recommends a systematic monitoring framework with easy-to-measure input, output and outcome indicators. The centre head acts as supervisor, mentor (friend, guide, role model) and monitor (checks progress, identifies problems, advises solutions).

Supervision is monitoring the performance of staff, noting merits and shortcomings and helping them improve — a process of stimulating growth. Benefits: fills gaps in knowledge and skills, helps understand ground realities, motivates teachers, builds the team, informs teachers of new guidelines and helps them relate to the community. Purposes: checking and advising on teaching-learning materials and the environment, promoting curriculum innovation, feedback on teacher performance, identifying staff development needs, quality checks, morale and professional support.

Monitoring is the continuous review of programme implementation through regular collection and analysis of data, to see that activities are on course and on schedule, inputs are well used, and problems are found and solved; the programme is adapted as children's needs change. Mentoring is a partnership of mutual benefit between mentor and mentee built on encouragement, openness, trust and respect; the mentor helps with specific issues, coaches skills, shares resources, challenges the mentee beyond the comfort zone, creates a safe space for risks and focuses on the mentee's total development.

Records are documented information that gives evidence of an activity. They help plan for each child, monitor progress in all domains, show the gap between expected and actual learning, communicate with families and the next school, evaluate planning, show accountability, prevent fraud and waste, and build good school-parent relations. Types: (1) children's records — profile or cumulative record (name, date of birth, sex, siblings, position in family, parents' names, qualifications, occupations, address, immunisation status, allergies, special needs), attendance register (home visit if a child is absent for days), checklists, portfolio of dated work, progress reports and observations; (2) staff records — personal details, qualifications, experience, date of joining, job description, salary, training, attendance with time sheet; (3) stock records — equipment, furniture and learning materials in store and used; (4) financial records — cash book (small day-to-day expenses), ledger (principal book with debit and credit columns and opening and closing balances), balance sheet (assets — current and long-term — and liabilities); (5) miscellaneous — safety inspection book, menu records, log books, prospectus, foundation documents, photographs, building plans, timetables, PTA minutes, visitor's book. Files should be labelled, coded, arranged subject-wise and locked.

Sources: grant-in-aid and mini-grants from government (e.g. Ministry of Women and Child Development, Social Welfare Board); community involvement — fairs and functions selling articles made by children and parents, volunteerism by skilled parents ('a penny saved is a penny earned'), renting out space after centre hours, donation camps for materials, toys and food grains, and donations and fees from parents.

Auditing helps staff form an opinion on the accuracy of financial statements, improves the accounting system and detects or prevents errors; audited accounts are submitted to funding bodies at the end of each financial year. Internal auditing: regular checks that transactions follow the budget and set procedures. External auditing: establishes the truth and fairness of accounts and compliance with statutes. Social accounting and auditing report the social and environmental effects of an organisation's actions; its main objective is effective use of resources, with a record of change, feedback, knowing what works and evidence for grants. Financial management covers procurement and allocation of funds and monitoring their use; preparing a budget — forecasting expenditure and estimating revenue to find the financing gap — is the first step of financial planning. Transactions are recorded promptly, reviewed monthly and audited externally each year.

vsa: What are the key functions shared by both management and administration?
Both are concerned with planning, organising and controlling — and with directing resources and people towards the goals of the ECCE centre.

or: What are the three levels of management typically found in an ECCE centre?
Top level — the owners of the centre; middle level — the centre head and assistants; first level — the ECCE staff and teachers.

vsa: What is the role of the head of an ECCE centre in supervision, mentoring and monitoring?

As supervisor the head checks staff performance and helps them improve; as mentor she acts as a friend, guide and role model; as monitor she checks overall and individual progress, identifies problems and advises solutions.

or: What are the benefits of supervision in an ECCE centre?

It fills gaps in teachers' knowledge and skills, helps understand ground realities and solve problems, motivates teachers, builds the team, makes teachers aware of new guidelines and helps them relate to the community.

vsa: Why is it necessary to document and keep records for all children? Give two reasons.

Any two: records build a picture of each child; they monitor progress in all domains and help plan the next steps; they show the gap between expected and actual learning; they help communicate with parents and the next school; they show accountability.

or: Personal details of each child with academic performance, assessments and results; school policies; minutes of meetings and information from the education department and other bodies; also admission registers, roll books, progress reports, staff, financial and stock records.

vsa: Records of all resources and materials at the centre — outdoor and indoor equipment, furniture, and learning materials such as story books, blocks, puzzles, crayons and paper — showing the quantity in store and the amount used; they are updated regularly.
What are the two types of auditing?

Internal auditing — regular, frequent checking of the centre's transactions and records to see they follow the budget and set procedures. External auditing — an outside check that establishes the truth and fairness of the accounts and their compliance with statutes.
The principal book or computer file of a centre for recording and totalling its economic transactions, with separate debit and credit columns and an opening and closing balance for each account.

sa: Why are cumulative records important? Describe a proforma for a cumulative record for children.

A cumulative record (child's profile), compiled with parents at admission, builds a full picture of each child, helps plan for the child's needs, track progress and communicate with parents and the next school. Proforma: name of the child; date of birth; sex; position in the family; number of siblings; father's name, qualification and occupation; mother's name, qualification and occupation; address and contact number; immunisation status; allergies, if any; specific needs of the child; any other relevant information.
What are the different types of records maintained in an ECCE centre?

Children's records (profile/cumulative record, attendance register, checklists, portfolio, progress reports, observations); staff records (personal details, qualifications, job description, salary, training, attendance); stock records (equipment, furniture, learning materials); financial records (cash book, ledger, balance sheet, fees, receipts, bank records); miscellaneous records (safety inspection book, menu, log books, prospectus, PTA minutes, visitor's book, photographs).
Differentiate between a cash book, a ledger and a balance sheet.

Cash book: a record of small, day-to-day purchases (stationery, cleaning material, ration) kept by a staff member before they are posted to the ledger. Ledger: the principal book or file recording and totalling all transactions, with debit and credit columns and opening and closing balances for each account. Balance sheet: a statement of the centre's financial position listing assets (current and long-term, such as cash, furniture, building) and then liabilities (current, such as salaries; long-term, such as loans).
Explain the importance of accounting and social auditing.

Social accounting and auditing record and report the social and environmental effects of an organisation's economic actions to interest groups and society. It checks performance against social, environmental and economic objectives and values. Objectives: effective use of resources; an ongoing record of how the centre has changed; feedback on how things are going; knowing what works well and what does not; knowing how far aims are achieved; and collecting information for grant applications and reports.
la: Discuss the importance of supervision, mentoring and monitoring in the management of an ECCE centre.

These sustain and improve the quality of services; the National ECCE Policy, 2013 asks for a systematic monitoring framework with input, output and outcome indicators, and the centre head plays all three roles. Supervision: monitoring staff performance, noting merits and shortcomings and helping them improve; it fills skill gaps, helps solve ground problems, motivates teachers, builds the team, spreads new guidelines, checks materials and the environment, gives feedback and professional support, and identifies training needs. Monitoring: continuous review of implementation with regular data collection; it checks whether inputs are well used and activities are on time, finds and solves problems, and adapts the programme to the changing needs of children and families. Mentoring: a trusting partnership of mutual benefit; the mentor helps on specific issues, coaches skills, shares resources, challenges the mentee, creates a safe space to take risks and focuses on total development.

la: Why are mobilisation and utilisation of resources important for an ECCE centre? Explain ways to raise funds.

All enterprises need funds, and expenses keep rising; a centre must raise enough money for building or rent, staff, materials, food and play equipment, and use it well through a budget, prompt records, monthly reviews and audits so that funds serve their purpose. Ways to raise funds: (1) grant-in-aid and mini-grants from government ministries and departments such as the Ministry of Women and Child Development and the Social Welfare Board; (2) fairs and cultural functions selling articles made by children and parents; (3) volunteerism — skilled parents and community members teach or make learning materials and toys; (4) renting out the space after centre hours for dance or art classes, or growing vegetables to sell; (5) donation camps for toys, clothes, stationery and food grains; (6) donations and fees from parents and other donors.
